rationale: The book's editorial title opens with the מִ֭שְׁלֵי construct chain (oshb:Prov.1.1), matching only one other verse-initial occurrence in the book, Prov.10.1 (mishle verse-initial: 2 of 915 verses). An infinitive-construct purpose chain follows, opening with לָדַ֣עַת "to know" at oshb:Prov.1.2 and recurring at Prov.1.3, Prov.1.4, and Prov.1.6, interrupted once by a hearer clause at Prov.1.5 (“that the wise man may hear, and increase in learning; that the man of understanding may attain to sound counsel;” web:Prov.1.5) before the whole opening closes on the motto “The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge, but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.” (web:Prov.1.7). The motto's closing word pair, skeleton חכמה ומוסר (oshb:Prov.1.7), repeats the purpose clause's own object skeleton from oshb:Prov.1.2, framing Prov.1.1-Prov.1.7 as one bracketed unit before the direct address to a son opens at Prov.1.8.
rejected_alternative: Treating Prov.1.1 as a standalone title verse, severed from the purpose clauses and the motto, was rejected because the infinitive chain of Prov.1.2-Prov.1.6 and the fear-of-Yahweh motto of Prov.1.7 form one connected editorial sentence running to the petuchah at Prov.1.7.
observed_substrate_signals: mishle verse-initial title formula at Prov.1.1 (2 of 915 verses book-wide)

device_notes: The title (Prov.1.1) is a bare construct chain, not itself parallelistic; the purpose clauses of Prov.1.2-Prov.1.6 pair their objects synonymously (wisdom and instruction; discernment and understanding), and the motto of Prov.1.7 closes the unit on an antithetic turn (the fear of Yahweh versus the fool who despises wisdom and instruction). No unit_type in the controlled vocabulary names an editorial title-plus-motto complex directly; instruction_lecture is used here as an approximate fit for the C1 opening frame, given the genre stretch involved.

rationale: A fresh imperative-plus-vocative opens the exordium, שְׁמַ֣ע בְּ֭נִי (oshb:Prov.1.8), directly after the petuchah that closes the title-and-motto complex (oshb:Prov.1.7 (petuchah, single-witness)). The rationale clause that follows, “for they will be a garland to grace your head, and chains around your neck.” (web:Prov.1.9), completes the appeal before a second, syntactically distinct vocative opens the temptation scenario at Prov.1.10 with its own conditional, בְּנִ֡י אִם (oshb:Prov.1.10).
rejected_alternative: Folding this exordium into the following temptation scenario, which continues through Prov.1.19, was considered, since both share the same speaker and addressee, but the fresh vocative-plus-conditional construction that opens Prov.1.10 marks a distinct rhetorical move and was kept as a separate row.

rationale clause (garland and chains imagery) at Prov.1.9
a second, distinct vocative-plus-conditional opening at Prov.1.10
device_notes: The appeal pairs synonymous parallelism across both verses: father's instruction and mother's teaching at Prov.1.8, garland and chains at Prov.1.9. This exordium spans two verses, shorter than the four-to-eight-verse span typical for instruction_lecture units elsewhere in this collection; the shortness reflects its function as a hinge between the title complex and the temptation scenario rather than a self-contained lesson.

rationale: The vocative that opened Prov.1.8 recurs with a conditional clause, בְּנִ֡י אִם יְפַתּ֥וּךָ "my son, if sinners entice you" (oshb:Prov.1.10), and the enticement is specified by a second protasis, אִם יֹאמְרוּ֮ "if they say" (oshb:Prov.1.11), introducing the sinners' own invitation in direct quotation. The quoted proposal runs through “You shall cast your lot among us. We'll all have one purse"-” (web:Prov.1.14), after which a fresh vocative resumes the father's own voice at Prov.1.15, marking the close of this unit.
rejected_alternative: Extending this unit through the father's application, which continues through Prov.1.19, was considered, since the quoted invitation and its rebuttal form one connected scenario, but the shift from the sinners' first-person-plural proposal to the father's renewed second-person vocative at Prov.1.15 marks a clean speech-frame seam and was kept as the boundary.

device_notes: Synonymous parallelism structures the sinners' own speech across Prov.1.11-Prov.1.14 (ambush and lurk, houses and plunder, lot and purse); the register is first-person plural ("let us") and shifts to the father's second-person address at Prov.1.15, which opens the next unit.

rationale: The father's direct address resumes with a fresh vocative and prohibition, בְּנִ֗י אַל תֵּלֵ֣ךְ "my son, don't walk" (oshb:Prov.1.15), applying the warning against the scenario quoted in Prov.1.11-Prov.1.14. A rationale clause follows at Prov.1.16, restated in summary form at the unit's close, “So are the ways of everyone who is greedy for gain. It takes away the life of its owners.” (web:Prov.1.19), the verse on which the petuchah falls (oshb:Prov.1.19 (petuchah, single-witness)).
rejected_alternative: Beginning this unit at Prov.1.16 instead of Prov.1.15 was considered, isolating the rationale clauses from the vocative that introduces them, but the fresh address is the stronger tier-1 seam and the two belong to the same application move.

device_notes: Antithetic and synonymous parallelism alternate across Prov.1.16-Prov.1.19 (feet that run to evil, a net spread in vain, an owner's life taken); the closing gnomic form generalizes the scenario into a proverb-like statement immediately before the petuchah.

rationale: Personified Wisdom becomes the subject and, from Prov.1.23, the speaker: “Wisdom calls aloud in the street. She utters her voice in the public squares.” (web:Prov.1.20), opening a public address that shifts from third-person narration (Prov.1.20-Prov.1.21) through a still-second/third-person indictment at Prov.1.22 — “"How long, you simple ones, will you love simplicity? How long will mockers delight themselves in mockery, and fools hate knowledge?” (web:Prov.1.22), where WEB opens its own curly quotation mark as an editorial signal (Tier-4-adjacent) rather than a Hebrew person-shift — to Wisdom's own first-person reproach, which the Hebrew itself begins at Prov.1.23 rather than 1.22: “Turn at my reproof. Behold, I will pour out my spirit on you. I will make known my words to you.” (web:Prov.1.23). The poem is bounded on both sides by petuchah: the preceding lecture closes at oshb:Prov.1.19 (petuchah, single-witness), and Wisdom's own address closes on “But whoever listens to me will dwell securely, and will be at ease, without fear of harm."” (web:Prov.1.33), the verse carrying the poem's own petuchah (oshb:Prov.1.33 (petuchah, single-witness)).
rejected_alternative: Splitting the poem at its internal shift from third-person narration (Prov.1.20-Prov.1.21) to Wisdom's own first-person reproach (from Prov.1.22) was considered, but the internal transition turns on a shift in grammatical person alone, without a fresh tier-1 speech-frame marker, and the connected speech act argues for one row.

device_notes: A ketiv/qere note attaches to the storm-word at Prov.1.27 (oshb:Prov.1.27, ketiv/qere, single-witness); the poem's own internal movement runs call (Prov.1.20-Prov.1.21), reproach (Prov.1.22-Prov.1.27), and consequence (Prov.1.28-Prov.1.33), with antithetic parallelism concentrated in the closing contrast between the one who listens and the disaster that overtakes the one who does not.

rationale: The chapter opens immediately after the petuchah that closes Wisdom's opening speech (oshb:Prov.1.33 (petuchah, single-witness)), with the chapter's one vocative, occurring once across its 22 verses, בְּ֭נִי אִם תִּקַּ֣ח 'my son, if you receive' (oshb:Prov.2.1), launching three protases (2.1, 2.3, 2.4: receive my words, cry out for understanding, seek her like silver) plus one purpose-infinitive clause (2.2: incline your ear to wisdom) running through Prov.2.4. The initial apodosis follows immediately, אָ֗ז תָּ֭בִין 'then you will understand' (oshb:Prov.2.5), naming the fear of Yahweh as the reward. Its opening word collates byte-identical against the word opening the second apodosis at oshb:Prov.2.9 (byte tier), which announces the same reward in terms of righteousness, justice, and equity. A purpose-clause pair follows on the same pattern: לְ֭הַצִּ֣ילְךָ 'to deliver you' opens Prov.2.12 (oshb:Prov.2.12), naming deliverance first from evil men (Prov.2.12-Prov.2.15) and then, in a byte-identical repetition of the same infinitive at oshb:Prov.2.16 (byte tier), from the strange woman (Prov.2.16-Prov.2.19). A concluding exhortation, לְמַ֗עַן 'therefore' (oshb:Prov.2.20), draws the chapter to its antithetic close, “But the wicked will be cut off from the land. The treacherous will be rooted out of it.” (web:Prov.2.22), the verse carrying the chapter's own petuchah (oshb:Prov.2.22 (petuchah, single-witness)).
rejected_alternative: A finer strophic split at the recurring 'then'/'to deliver you' markers (Prov.2.1-Prov.2.4, Prov.2.5-Prov.2.11, Prov.2.12-Prov.2.19, Prov.2.20-Prov.2.22) was considered and is textually real, but the chapter's vocative fires exactly once across its 22 verses and the chapter is grammatically one long sentence from protasis to conclusion, so it is kept as one row at some cost to the four-to-eight-verse span typical for instruction_lecture units elsewhere in this collection.

device_notes: Ketiv/qere notes attach to two verses inside this span: oshb:Prov.2.7 and oshb:Prov.2.8 (both ketiv/qere, single-witness), sitting inside the first apodosis section. The protasis clauses of Prov.2.1-Prov.2.4 and the apodosis clauses of Prov.2.5-Prov.2.11 run on synonymous parallelism, restating one recurring appeal and one recurring reward in parallel cola, with the closing couplet turning antithetic (Prov.2.21-Prov.2.22: the upright remain in the land, but the wicked are cut off).

rationale: בְּ֭נִי (oshb:Prov.3.1) opens both the row and the part, the first of four bni_address occurrences within the part, recurring at 3.21, 4.10, and 4.20 (bni_address inventory: 22 tokens book-wide, four heading this part). Two imperative-plus-consequence couplets follow: retain the father's teaching for length of days (3.1-3.2), then bind kindness and truth on the heart for favor with God and man (3.3-3.4). The row closes at the petuchah after Prov.3.4 (oshb:Prov.3.4, single-witness), where אֱלֹהִ֣ים (oshb:Prov.3.4) is the divine name named once; the couplets beginning at 3.5 each name the divine name יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Prov.3.5) directly, while neither couplet in 3.1-3.4 does.
rejected_alternative: Extending the row through 3.12 was rejected because the couplets from 3.5 onward each name the divine name יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Prov.3.5) directly, a naming shift the petuchah at 3.4 (oshb:Prov.3.4, single-witness) corroborates but does not itself drive.

device_notes: Synonymous parallelism binds each couplet's two half-lines -- teaching and commandments at web:Prov.3.1 “My son, don’t forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments,” and kindness and truth at 3.3; the neck-and-heart-tablet figure of 3.3 gives the abstract virtue pair a concrete, wearable image.

rationale: From 3.5 through 3.12 four imperative-plus-consequence couplets each name the divine name -- trust (3.5-3.6), fear and turn from evil (3.7-3.8), honor with substance (3.9-3.10), and accept discipline (3.11-3.12): the divine name is named once each in 3.5, 3.7, 3.9, 3.11, 3.12 (5 tokens across the row's 8 verses), absent from 3.6, 3.8, 3.10, a naming density that sets these couplets apart from the teaching-retention pair of 3.1-3.4, where the divine name is named only once, as אֱלֹהִ֣ים (oshb:Prov.3.4). The petuchah after Prov.3.10 (oshb:Prov.3.10, single-witness) falls inside the row, between the honor couplet and the discipline couplet, without ending it: both keep the same imperative-plus-consequence shape and both name the divine name, so the mark corroborates an internal pause rather than the row's own edge. The row ends before 3.13, where the address shifts from second-person imperative to a third-person beatitude formula.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the row at the petuchah after 3.10 (oshb:Prov.3.10, single-witness) was considered and set aside: the honor couplet before it and the discipline couplet after it keep the same construction and both name the divine name (יְ֭הוָה, oshb:Prov.3.9; יְ֭הוָה, oshb:Prov.3.11), so the mark falls inside one naming-density unit rather than at its edge.
observed_substrate_signals: the divine name is named once each in 3.5, 3.7, 3.9, 3.11, 3.12 (5 tokens across the row's 8 verses; word-bound accent_stripped sweep restricted to the row's own span), absent from 3.6, 3.8, 3.10
petuchah after Prov.3.10 (single-witness, internal to the row)

device_notes: Each couplet pairs synonymous halves (trust/lean at 3.5, fear/turn at 3.7); the fourth couplet (3.11-3.12) varies the pattern with a father-son simile rather than a bodily-benefit result, a texture shift within the shared construction.

rationale: The row opens with אַשְׁרֵ֣י (oshb:Prov.3.13) governing 'the man' in third person, a genre break from the second-person imperative address running since 3.1 -- the tier-1 signal opening the poem the strategy flags as a bounds-argue candidate. The praise of wisdom continues through 3.18, which closes with מְאֻשָּֽׁר (oshb:Prov.3.18), a participle sharing the same root as the opening אַשְׁרֵ֣י and forming a root-level inclusio around the personal-benefit half of the poem (more precious than jewels, length of days, riches, pleasant paths, a tree of life). The petuchah after Prov.3.18 (oshb:Prov.3.18, single-witness) falls at that inclusio's close. The couplet at 3.19-3.20 extends the poem from personal benefit to cosmic scope -- יְֽהוָ֗ה (oshb:Prov.3.19) founding the earth and establishing the heavens by wisdom and understanding -- before the row ends at the return to second-person address at 3.21.
rejected_alternative: Ending the row at 3.18, with the petuchah there (oshb:Prov.3.18, single-witness) as the boundary, was considered and set aside: 3.19-3.20 continue third-person wisdom-praise rather than opening a new address, so the mark reads as an internal inclusio-close rather than the poem's outer edge.

device_notes: Synonymous parallelism describes wisdom's value in 3.14-3.17 (profit/return, precious/incomparable, right hand/left hand, pleasantness/peace); 3.19-3.20 shifts to a synthetic pair (earth-founding building on heaven-establishing) rather than synonymous restatement, marking the poem's move from human benefit to cosmology.

rationale: בְּ֭נִי (oshb:Prov.3.21) reopens second-person address at 3.21, the part's second lecture-opening slot (matching 3.1, 4.10, 4.20). The row keeps sound wisdom and discretion before the addressee's eyes as one extended promise: life and grace (3.21-3.22), secure walking and untroubled sleep (3.23-3.24), and freedom from sudden fear because יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Prov.3.26) is the addressee's confidence (3.25-3.26). No petuchah or other disclosure-object note falls inside this span; the row ends before 3.27, where the object of each admonition shifts from the addressee's own wisdom-keeping to the addressee's neighbor.
rejected_alternative: A narrower cut after 3.24, separating the wisdom-admonition (3.21-3.24) from the fear-admonition (3.25-3.26), lacks any parashah or disclosure-object support, and both halves keep the same second-person, self-directed object, so the wider bound is kept instead.

device_notes: Synonymous parallelism (eyes, מֵעֵינֶ֑יךָ, oshb:Prov.3.21, continuing into life/grace at 3.22; lying down/sleep at 3.24); only 1 of 3 admonition-plus-consequence movements in this row -- the closing one (3.25-3.26) -- names the divine name יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Prov.3.26) explicitly as the ground of confidence, a slight intensification toward the row's close.

rationale: Five consecutive prohibition imperatives open at 3.27 and run through 3.31, each addressing conduct toward another party -- withholding good from its owner (3.27), delaying a neighbor's due (3.28), plotting against a neighbor (3.29), needless strife (3.30), and envy of a violent man (3.31) -- a list-register run distinguishing this unit from the self-directed wisdom-keeping of 3.21-3.26. Three of the five verses carry ketiv/qere notes (3.27, 3.28, 3.30) and 3.28 also carries a paseq, all single-witness disclosure objects internal to the row; none functions as a boundary driver. The row ends before 3.32, where a two-letter conjunction introduces a shift from second-person prohibition to third-person gnomic rationale.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the five-verse prohibition list into narrower pairs (for example 3.27-3.28 / 3.29-3.31) was considered and set aside: no parashah or disclosure object marks an interior boundary, and all five verses share one prohibition-imperative construction. Reading 3.27 as a tov-min ('better than') comparative is a mandated rival to disclose: 3.27 is itself a ketiv/qere verse (oshb:Prov.3.27, disclosed above), and its contiguous טוב מ skeleton pairs with a source-marked object ('withhold good from its owner') rather than the comparative construction shared by the sweep's three other hits, Prov.15.16, Prov.16.8, and Prov.16.16.

device_notes: The prohibition series varies its grammatical object across the five verses (owner, neighbor twice, opponent, violent man) while keeping the prohibition-imperative shape constant, a construction-run cohesion rather than a shared-theme cluster.

rationale: A two-letter conjunction (oshb:Prov.3.32) opens 3.32 and shifts the discourse from the second-person prohibition series of 3.27-3.31 to four third-person gnomic statements pairing the divine name's disposition (יְהוָ֣ה, oshb:Prov.3.32; יְ֭הוָה, oshb:Prov.3.33) with a human outcome: abomination versus friendship (3.32), curse versus blessing (3.33), mockery versus grace (3.34), and glory versus shame (3.35). The row closes at the petuchah after Prov.3.35 (oshb:Prov.3.35, single-witness), the last verse before chapter 4 opens with a plural address at 4.1.
rejected_alternative: Folding 3.32-3.35 into the same unit as 3.27-3.31 was set aside: the conjunction opening 3.32 (oshb:Prov.3.32) marks a discourse turn to rationale-giving, and the shift from second-person imperative to third-person gnomic statement is a construction change the shared 'conduct toward another' theme alone would not justify keeping together.

rationale: שִׁמְע֣וּ בָ֭נִים (oshb:Prov.4.1) ('listen, sons') opens chapter 4 with a plural address, distinct from the singular address term shared by 3 of 4 lecture-openers in this part (3.1, 3.21, 4.10, 4.20). The row sets up a father's instruction (4.1-4.2), then recounts his own childhood as an only son (4.3) before introducing his own father's reported words with וַיֹּ֥אמֶר לִ֗י (oshb:Prov.4.4) ('and he said to me') in 4.4, a speech-frame device that itself completes one admonition-plus-consequence couplet. The row ends there, before the quoted instruction's own imperative pair opens fresh at 4.5.
rejected_alternative: Keeping 4.1-4.9 as one unit was considered: nothing marks 4.4/4.5 with a parashah or disclosure object, so the seam rests on the speech-frame device alone (וַיֹּ֥אמֶר לִ֗י (oshb:Prov.4.4)) rather than corroborated tier-1-plus-tier-3 evidence, which is why this boundary is held at lower confidence rather than folded together.
observed_substrate_signals: שִׁמְע֣וּ בָ֭נִים (oshb:Prov.4.1) plural address opening 4.1, unlike the singular address elsewhere in this part
autobiographical frame at 4.3 ('I was a son to my father')
reported-speech frame וַיֹּ֥אמֶר לִ֗י (oshb:Prov.4.4) within 4.4, introducing quoted paternal instruction
the row's own front seam, Prov.3.35, carries a petuchah (oshb:Prov.3.35, single-witness) belonging to the previous unit; beyond it, the row's own four verses carry no further disclosure-object note
device_notes: The mise-en-abyme structure (a father quoting his own father) is a structure not repeated elsewhere in this part's rows; synonymous parallelism continues in 4.1-4.2 (listen/pay attention; instruction/understanding).

rationale: The quoted paternal instruction introduced at the close of 4.4 continues here with a fresh imperative pair, קְנֵ֣ה חָ֭כְמָה קְנֵ֣ה בִינָ֑ה (oshb:Prov.4.5) ('get wisdom, get understanding'), echoed again within 4.7 (oshb:Prov.4.7) -- split as קְנֵ֣ה חָכְמָ֑ה (4.7's 3rd-4th words) and קְנֵ֣ה בִינָֽה (4.7's final two words), divided by וּבְכָל קִ֝נְיָנְךָ֗ -- an internal repetition bracketing 4.5-4.7 before the row closes with wisdom personified as a figure who exalts, honors, and crowns the one who embraces her (4.8-4.9). No disclosure object falls inside this span. The row ends before the part's third lecture-opener at 4.10.
rejected_alternative: Splitting 4.5-4.7 from the personification lines of 4.8-4.9 was considered and set aside: the repeated קְנֵ֣ה חָ֭כְמָה קְנֵ֣ה בִינָ֑ה (oshb:Prov.4.5) imperative and the result clauses that follow it read as one continuous appeal rather than two, so no interior seam is argued here.

Within 6:20-23 itself the parashah layer stays silent; the next petuchah in sequence sits at 6:26, inside the following unit, so this internal seam rests on the vocative restart and metaphor-closure argued above rather than on parashah corroboration.

rationale: The infinitive-of-purpose clause "לִ֭שְׁמָרְךָ מֵאֵ֣שֶׁת רָ֑ע..." (oshb:Prov.6.24; “to keep you from the immoral woman”, web:Prov.6.24) governs the whole span: it states the aim, 6:25 issues the matching prohibition (do not lust after her beauty), 6:26 supplies the causal warrant (a prostitute reduces you to a loaf of bread), and 6:27-28 supply a paired rhetorical-question analogy (fire in the lap, walking on coals) that 6:29 applies directly back to the purpose clause's subject: "כֵּ֗ן הַ֭בָּא אֶל אֵ֣שֶׁת רֵעֵ֑הוּ..." (oshb:Prov.6.29; “So is he who goes in to his neighbor's wife”, web:Prov.6.29). The unit closes there, before 6:30 opens an unrelated comparison subject, the thief. This governing infinitive-of-purpose is itself the syntactic continuation of the preceding row's closing motive clause at 6:23 (oshb:Prov.6.23), not an independently introduced topic; the resulting 6:23/6:24 seam lacks a vocative-restart of its own, and the parashah layer stays silent there too, with the nearest petuchah marks sitting at oshb:Prov.6.19, before the unit, and oshb:Prov.6.26, inside this row's own span.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the fire-and-coals rhetorical questions (6:27-29) into their own row was rejected because they supply the warrant for the prohibition of 6:24-26 under one governing purpose clause, not an independent topic. The petuchah at 6:26 is disclosed as tier-3 corroboration for a possible 6:20-26/6:27-35 split, but the governing purpose infinitive opened at 6:24 argues against treating 6:26 as the operative seam.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Prov.6.24 infinitive-of-purpose opener "לִ֭שְׁמָרְךָ מֵאֵ֣שֶׁת רָ֑ע"

device_notes: Synthetic-to-applied argument structure (purpose, prohibition, warrant, analogy, application); the fire/coals pair in 6:27-28 is the unit's rhetorical-question figure. A petuchah is attested at 6:26 in WLC (tier-3 corroboration, single witness); it falls inside this span rather than at its edge and is disclosed here rather than treated as the boundary driver, per the governing-clause argument above.

rationale: "לֹא יָב֣וּזוּ לַ֭גַּנָּב..." (oshb:Prov.6.30; “Men don't despise a thief...”, web:Prov.6.30) opens a new comparison subject: a thief who steals from hunger draws some social allowance and owes restitution (6:30-31), but the adulterer, unlike the thief, “is void of understanding” and “destroys his own soul” (web:Prov.6.32), facing wounds, dishonor, and a husband's unrelenting jealousy that “won't spare in the day of vengeance” and “won't regard any ransom” (web:Prov.6.34-35). The a fortiori argument (lesser case, thief, versus greater case, adulterer) is confined to these six verses and closes the chapter at the petuchah of 6:35, before the next lecture reopens at 7:1 outside this part.
rejected_alternative: Reading 6:30-35 as a single_proverb was rejected because the thief-versus-adulterer comparison unfolds across paired clauses building one a fortiori argument, not one couplet; treating it as a numerical_saying was also rejected, since no x-of-y count governs the span.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Prov.6.30 subject-shift opener "לֹא יָב֣וּזוּ לַ֭גַּנָּב"
oshb:Prov.6.31 restitution clause (sevenfold repayment)
oshb:Prov.6.32 contrast clause, adulterer "void of understanding"
oshb:Prov.6.34-6.35 vengeance/ransom closing pair
device_notes: Synthetic, comparative argument structure (lesser-to-greater case); the thief/adulterer pairing is the unit's organizing figure, not an antithetic couplet. A petuchah closes 6:35 in WLC (tier-3 corroboration, single witness), matching the chapter-end boundary; 6:29 is cited here to mark where the preceding unit's application clause ends, not as evidence internal to this span.

rationale: The address opens with the vocative בְּ֭נִי (oshb:Prov.7.1), the start of a fresh charge right after the petuchah at oshb:Prov.6.35 (petuchah, single-witness) that closes the prior lecture. The purpose clause of web:Prov.7.5 keeps the son “from the strange woman, from the foreigner who flatters with her words”, and that clause is picked up by the causal כִּ֭י opening oshb:Prov.7.6, so the window-scene report reads as the ground for it rather than a fresh unit; the particle וְהִנֵּ֣ה at oshb:Prov.7.10 then marks the narrative's own internal turn, introducing the woman's approach within the same first-person report. Her quoted invitation (Prov.7.14-20) and its narrated outcome (Prov.7.21-23) continue that one illustrative movement without a further byte-level break. The span closes at the petuchah in oshb:Prov.7.23 (petuchah, single-witness), where the image of the arrow striking the liver ends the report, and “doesn’t know that it will cost his life” (web:Prov.7.23) gives the narrator's own verdict on the scene just before plural direct address resumes at web:Prov.7.24.
rejected_alternative: A split isolating Prov.7.1-7.5 from the window scene was considered, but the causal כִּ֭י opening Prov.7.6 grounds the narrated scene in the purpose clause of 7.5 rather than starting a fresh unit there.

device_notes: 7.1-4 pair synonymous cola (keep my words / lay up my commandments; bind them on your fingers / write them on the tablet of your heart), the address form shared with the earlier chs.1-6 lectures; once the report opens at 7.6 the cola mostly carry sequential narrative action -- window, street, twilight, encounter -- rather than balanced parallel members. The closing simile chain at 7.22-23 (ox to the slaughter, fool stepping into a noose, bird hurrying to the snare, arrow through the liver) piles figures in successive cola to dramatize the young man's failure to read his own danger.

rationale: Plural direct address resumes at “Now therefore, sons, listen to me” (web:Prov.7.24; Hebrew וְעַתָּ֣ה בָ֭נִים שִׁמְעוּ לִ֑י, oshb:Prov.7.24), echoing the singular vocative בְּ֭נִי that opened the lecture at oshb:Prov.7.1 and bracketing the inset narrative that just closed at the petuchah in oshb:Prov.7.23 (petuchah, single-witness). The closing quatrain runs through Prov.7.27, itself marked by a petuchah (oshb:Prov.7.27, petuchah, single-witness) that also ends the chapter; “Her house is the way to Sheol” (web:Prov.7.27) restates the lecture's danger in one closing image rather than opening new material, so the span holds together as the frame's second bracket.
rejected_alternative: Extending this span back to include the narrated outcome of Prov.7.21-23 was considered, but the return to plural direct address at 7.24 marks a fresh discourse frame -- corroborated by the petuchah at Prov.7.23 -- that closes the lecture rather than continuing the narrative report.
observed_substrate_signals: opening formula וְעַתָּ֣ה בָ֭נִים שִׁמְעוּ לִ֑י at oshb:Prov.7.24 shares its wording with the vocative frame that opens the lecture at 7.1
petuchah at Prov.7.23 (single-witness) marks the seam into this closing quatrain
petuchah at Prov.7.27 (single-witness) closes chapter 7
imperative mood returns at 7.24-25 after the narrated third-person report of 7.6-23
device_notes: 7.25-26 pairs synthetic escalation (don't let your heart turn to her ways / don't go astray in her paths, then she has thrown down many wounded / her slain form a mighty army), climbing to the closing figure of 7.27, where her house becomes the road to Sheol going down to the chambers of death -- a spatial image answering the window-and-house imagery that opened the report at 7.6-8.

rationale: The chapter opens in the third person -- “Doesn’t wisdom cry out” (web:Prov.8.1; Hebrew הֲלֹֽא חָכְמָ֥ה תִקְרָ֑א וּ֝תְבוּנָ֗ה תִּתֵּ֥ן קוֹלָֽהּ, oshb:Prov.8.1) -- describing wisdom crying out at the gates before her own first-person call begins at web:Prov.8.4, “I call to you men” (web:Prov.8.4). The shift from that third-person description to wisdom's own voice at אֲלֵיכֶ֣ם, “to you” (oshb:Prov.8.4), is the content of the very cry the narrator has just introduced in 8.1-3, so the setup and the call proper form one speech-event rather than two. The call moves from the appeal to hear (8.4-11, closing “wisdom is better than rubies” at web:Prov.8.11) into wisdom's self-commendation of her gifts, opened by the declaration אֲֽנִי חָ֭כְמָה (“I, wisdom,” oshb:Prov.8.12), continuing the same first-person voice opened at 8.4 rather than opening a fresh address, and the span runs to the petuchah at oshb:Prov.8.21 (petuchah, single-witness), where “I fill their treasuries” (web:Prov.8.21) closes the gift-commendation just before the cosmological turn of Prov.8.22.
rejected_alternative: Separating the self-declaration at Prov.8.12 from the preceding call to hear (8.1-11) was considered, but the declaration אֲֽנִי חָ֭כְמָה (oshb:Prov.8.12) continues the same first-person voice wisdom opened at 8.4 straight through to the petuchah at Prov.8.21, staying in that voice rather than returning to third-person narration or reopening with a fresh address formula.
observed_substrate_signals: petuchah at Prov.7.27 (single-witness) precedes the chapter's opening narrator frame

a ketiv/qere note at oshb:Prov.8.17 (single-witness) is a live inline-ketiv site within the self-commendation: the qere אֹהֲבַ֣י (matching “those who love me” in web:Prov.8.17) stands against the unpointed ketiv אהביה preceding it in the bytes, a person/voice-bearing variant
petuchah at Prov.8.21 (single-witness) closes the gift-commendation before the cosmological material of 8.22
device_notes: 8.1-3 narrates wisdom's public cry before the first-person call of 8.4 begins; 8.4-11 and 8.12-21 both run mainly as synthetic parallelism building toward a climactic line (wisdom is better than rubies at 8.11; I fill their treasuries at 8.21) rather than antithetic contrast -- a hymn-like register distinct from the couplet-by-couplet sentences of chs.10-29.

rationale: The grammatical subject shifts at the seam: Yahweh, not wisdom's own "I," opens the clause -- “Yahweh possessed me in the beginning of his work” (web:Prov.8.22; Hebrew יְֽהוָ֗ה קָ֭נָנִי רֵאשִׁ֣ית, oshb:Prov.8.22) -- right after the petuchah at oshb:Prov.8.21 (petuchah, single-witness) that closed the gift-commendation. A chain of temporal clauses (before, when, while) then narrates wisdom's place before and during creation, running through Prov.8.29's boundary-setting of the sea to Prov.8.30's craftsman image and closing at web:Prov.8.31, “rejoicing in his whole world” (web:Prov.8.31), which the petuchah at oshb:Prov.8.31 (petuchah, single-witness) marks off from the renewed address opening Prov.8.32.
rejected_alternative: Treating Prov.8.22-31 as a continuation of the gift-commendation rather than its own movement was considered, but the shift to Yahweh as grammatical subject at 8.22 together with the petuchah at Prov.8.21 mark a fresh section beginning with the creation account.
observed_substrate_signals: petuchah at Prov.8.21 (single-witness) opens this span's front seam
subject shift to Yahweh at the opening clause of oshb:Prov.8.22, יְֽהוָ֗ה קָ֭נָנִי רֵאשִׁ֣ית
paseq at Prov.8.29 and Prov.8.30 (single-witness; a bare count entry, not a positional claim)
petuchah at Prov.8.31 (single-witness) closes the cosmological movement before 8.32 resumes direct address
device_notes: 8.22-29 strings temporal clauses (before the mountains, when he established the heavens, when he set a circle on the deep) describing what did or did not yet exist stage by stage in the creation account -- a synthetic, narrative-shaped parallelism distinct from the address-form couplets bracketing it. 8.30-31 turns to two cola of synonymous rejoicing (a delight day by day, “always rejoicing before him” (web:Prov.8.30) / rejoicing in his whole world, my delight was with the sons of men).

rationale: Direct address returns with “Now therefore, my sons, listen to me” (web:Prov.8.32; Hebrew וְעַתָּ֣ה בָ֭נִים שִׁמְעוּ לִ֑י, oshb:Prov.8.32), a four-word summons attested at three sites book-wide (sweep: 3 verses, skeleton tier -- oshb:Prov.5.7, oshb:Prov.7.24, oshb:Prov.8.32) as a recurring lecture-transition formula rather than wording unique to this seam. What marks 8.32 as this poem's own closing frame is not the wording itself but what follows it: the summons opens directly on the petuchah at oshb:Prov.8.31 (petuchah, single-witness) that ended the cosmological account, and the beatitude form of 8.32-34 gives way to the antithesis closing the chapter: “whoever finds me finds life” (web:Prov.8.35; a ketiv/qere note attaches to oshb:Prov.8.35, single-witness) against “those who hate me love death” (web:Prov.8.36), set life against death in the span's own final couplet at the petuchah in oshb:Prov.8.36 (petuchah, single-witness), which also closes the chapter.
rejected_alternative: Keeping Prov.8.32-36 attached to the cosmological account that precedes it was considered, but the petuchah at Prov.8.31 opens directly onto the beatitude-then-antithesis movement closing the chapter, which the four-word summons -- a recurring lecture-transition formula -- introduces rather than distinguishes.
observed_substrate_signals: opening formula וְעַתָּ֣ה בָ֭נִים שִׁמְעוּ לִ֑י at oshb:Prov.8.32 is a recurring lecture-transition formula, attested at three sites book-wide (sweep: 3 verses, skeleton tier -- oshb:Prov.5.7, oshb:Prov.7.24, oshb:Prov.8.32)
petuchah at Prov.8.31 (single-witness) marks the seam into this closing movement

device_notes: 8.32-34 pairs beatitude form with imperative address (hear instruction, and be wise; watching daily at my gates, waiting at my door posts), and 8.35-36 closes with antithetic parallelism (whoever finds me finds life / he who sins against me wrongs his own soul), setting life against death in the chapter's final couplet -- the poem's own inclusio answer to the beatitude that opened the call at 8.32-34.

rationale: Prov.9.1 opens third-person narration whose subject is personified Wisdom (חכמות, oshb:Prov.9.1), building her house and hewing her seven pillars; the same figure prepares the meal in 9:2 and sends her maidens to call out in 9:3, and their call becomes her own quoted summons in 9:4-6, closing on “Walk in the way of understanding.” (web:Prov.9.6) That imperative answers the invitation the scene opened with. Prov.9.7 changes both subject and mode, dropping the personified figure for anonymous participial sayings about correcting a mocker, so the span is held to 9:6.
rejected_alternative: Extending the span through 9:9 to align with the petuchah recorded there was rejected: the mark falls after a discourse break that has already occurred at 9:7, so it corroborates the following unit's close, not this one's.
observed_substrate_signals: personified subject חכמות (oshb:Prov.9.1) governs the verbs of 9:1-9:3 and speaks the quoted invitation of 9:4-9:6
the petuchah at Prov.8.36 (single-witness) sits at the front seam, immediately before this span opens
device_notes: Narrative-to-direct-speech progression (third-person build/prepare/send, then Wisdom's own first-person invitation); synthetic, not antithetic — no wicked/righteous contrast pair occurs in this span.

rationale: This span pivots from the banquet scene to a short run built on second-person imperatives: 9:8’s “Don’t reprove a scoffer... Reprove a wise person” and 9:9’s “Instruct a wise person... Teach a righteous person” (web:Prov.9.8, web:Prov.9.9) bracket the participial maxim of 9:7 about a corrector's reward. The imperative core (אל תוכח, oshb:Prov.9.8, skeleton tier; תן, הודע, oshb:Prov.9.9, skeleton tier) marks a different mood from the declarative maxims that follow at 9:10, where the verbs turn conditional and nominal.
rejected_alternative: Treating 9:7-9:12 as one combined unit was rejected: 9:8-9:9 carry second-person imperatives addressed to a hearer, while 9:10-9:12 shift to nominal and conditional maxims without an imperative verb, a mood boundary the petuchah at 9:9 corroborates.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative verb הוכח (oshb:Prov.9.8, skeleton tier) and תן / הודע (oshb:Prov.9.9, skeleton tier) frame the participial opening of 9:7
petuchah at Prov.9.9 (single-witness) falls at this span's own closing verse
device_notes: Participle-imperative-imperative sequence; the mocker/wise-person contrast is synonymous rather than antithetic (no adversative clause structure), a texture distinct from the antithetic bicola that dominate the following collection. This admonition_unit stands outside C1's instruction_lecture/wisdom_poem default by the imperative core named above, not by exception.

rationale: 9:10's nominal thesis — the fear of Yahweh as wisdom's beginning — opens a short run without an imperative verb, continuing in 9:11 with a first-person clause, “For by me your days will be multiplied” (web:Prov.9.11), that returns to Wisdom's own voice from 9:1-6, and closing in 9:12's conditional maxim about bearing one's own wisdom or mockery. Prov.9.13 then introduces a different subject, a foolish woman, ending this run before that shift.
rejected_alternative: Folding 9:10-9:12 into the following Woman Folly scene was rejected: 9:13 introduces a new grammatical subject that 9:10-9:12's fear-of-Yahweh and self-benefit maxims do not carry.
observed_substrate_signals: no imperative verb governs 9:10-9:12, a shift away from the imperative core of 9:8-9:9
first-person בי ("by me", oshb:Prov.9.11) recurs the personified voice of 9:1-9:6 after the intervening third-person maxims of 9:7-9:9
the petuchah at the immediately preceding verse, Prov.9.9 (single-witness), sits at this span's front seam
device_notes: Nominal thesis followed by first-person and conditional clauses; the adversative "but"-clause typical of the surrounding admonition unit and the following sentence collection drops out of this span.

rationale: 9:13 introduces a new subject, the foolish woman (אשת כסילות, oshb:Prov.9.13), and the same figure carries the action through her seating at the city gate in 9:14, her call to passersby in 9:15, and her quoted invitation in 9:16-17, closing in 9:18 on the narrator's verdict that her guests are in Sheol's depths. The invitation formula of 9:16, “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here” (web:Prov.9.16), repeats the bare consonants מי פתי יסר הנה (oshb:Prov.9.16) already spoken by Wisdom at Prov.9.4, marking this span as the deliberate counter-scene to 9:1-6 rather than a continuation of the intervening sayings of 9:7-9:12.
rejected_alternative: Splitting off 9:17 as a standalone saying was rejected: it continues Folly's own direct speech opened in 9:16, keeping the same subject and addressee.
observed_substrate_signals: new grammatical subject אשת כסילות (oshb:Prov.9.13) governs 9:13-9:15 and speaks the quoted invitation of 9:16-9:17
the invitation formula of 9:16 shares its opening four consonantal words with Prov.9.4
petuchah at Prov.9.18 (single-witness) closes this span and the collection it belongs to
device_notes: Mirror-image envelope to 9:1-6 (seat/call/invite structure); the antithesis sits in outcome alone (this table ends in Sheol, the other in understanding), not in a verse-internal "but"-clause.

rationale: Prov.10.1 opens with the second verse-initial משלי (mishle, oshb:Prov.10.1) heading in the book — the collection-seam inventory records exactly two such hits book-wide, at Prov.1.1 and here — and the same verse continues as a complete antithetic bicolon contrasting a wise son who gladdens his father with a foolish son who grieves his mother. The header and the proverb share one clause; nothing marks a break between the title-word and the son/father/mother saying that follows it.
rejected_alternative: Reading 10:1 as a bare title separate from its own proverb body was rejected: the wise-son/foolish-son antithesis sits in the same clause as the heading, not in an added unit.
observed_substrate_signals: verse-initial משלי token (oshb:Prov.10.1), the second of exactly two hits book-wide per the collection-seam inventory (the other is Prov.1.1)
petuchah at this verse and at the immediately preceding verse Prov.9.18 (both single-witness) bracket the C1/C2 seam
device_notes: Antithetic bicolon (glad father / grieving mother) fused to a title-word opening; the header function and the sentence collection's default unit coincide in one verse.

rationale: 10:2 contrasts ill-gotten treasure, which profits nothing, with righteousness, which delivers from death — a complete antithetic bicolon on its own subject pair. The rescue-from-death B-line recurs at Prov.11.4 later in this same part, but not adjacently, so it corroborates a recurring formula rather than a local pairing with either of this verse's own neighbors. The petuchah at the immediately preceding verse, Prov.10.1, is the mishle header's own mark and does not extend into this verse's own boundary.
rejected_alternative: Clustering with 10:3 was set aside: that verse introduces Yahweh as grammatical agent, a different construction from this verse's impersonal treasure/righteousness contrast.
observed_substrate_signals: antithetic bicolon opposing אוצרות רשע (treasures of wickedness) and צדקה (righteousness), oshb:Prov.10.2
the B-line וצדקה תציל ממות (oshb:Prov.10.2, "but righteousness delivers from death") recurs word-for-word at Prov.11.4
device_notes: Antithetic parallelism; the wealth/righteousness pairing recurs across the sentence collection without adjacency-based cohesion here.

rationale: 10:3 names Yahweh as the grammatical agent who keeps the righteous soul from hunger while thrusting away the wicked's desire, a distinct construction from the abstract-quality contrasts on either side of it.
rejected_alternative: No cluster forms with 10:2 or 10:4: neither shares Yahweh as subject, and the hunger/desire pairing here is not picked up by either neighbor's own imagery.
observed_substrate_signals: Yahweh (יהוה, oshb:Prov.10.3) is the explicit grammatical subject of both clauses, unlike the impersonal constructions in 10:2 and 10:4
device_notes: Antithetic bicolon with a named divine agent, a construction that recurs elsewhere in the chapter without standing adjacent to this verse (this chapter's own YHWH-density texture).

rationale: 10:4 contrasts the poverty produced by a lazy hand with the wealth produced by a diligent hand — a hand-imagery bicolon distinct from 10:3's hunger/desire pairing and from 10:5's summer-gathering image.
rejected_alternative: Reading 10:4-10:5 as one unit on the strength of their shared diligence/laziness theme was rejected: neither verse's wording (hand imagery here, season imagery there) recurs in the other, so the link is topical rather than lexical.
observed_substrate_signals: hand-construct pair כף רמיה ("slack hand") / יד חרוצים ("hand of the diligent"), oshb:Prov.10.4
device_notes: Antithetic bicolon built on a body-part metonymy (hand); no lexical overlap with the following verse's harvest imagery.

rationale: 10:5 contrasts a son who gathers in summer with one who sleeps through harvest, recalling the wise-son/foolish-son pair of 10:1 by role-word alone; the two verses do not share wording beyond that common noun, and three unrelated sayings intervene.
rejected_alternative: Treating this verse as continuing 10:1's son-pair was rejected: the shared noun בן ("son") recurs across the whole collection and the two verses are not adjacent, so no catchword chain links them.
observed_substrate_signals: seasonal-labor pair אגר בקיץ ("gathers in summer") / נרדם בקציר ("sleeps in harvest"), oshb:Prov.10.5
device_notes: Antithetic bicolon; agricultural-calendar imagery distinct from the surrounding body-part and speech-organ metaphors.

rationale: 10:6 sets blessings on the righteous head against violence covering the wicked mouth. The B-line, ופי רשעים יכסה חמס (oshb:Prov.10.6), reappears word for word at Prov.10.11, five verses on, but nothing in the adjacent 10:7 picks up either the head/blessing or mouth/violence pairing.

rationale: This is one of the collection's better-than sayings: a comparative particle (min, than) governs the whole sentence rather than a waw-adversative splitting two independent clauses. Being lightly esteemed with a servant is set as preferable to self-honoring while lacking bread -- one comparison, not a two-subject antithesis.

rationale: A righteous person's regard for an animal's need opens the verse; the waw then turns to the wicked, whose mercies are themselves called cruel -- an ironic pairing of a compassion-word with a cruelty-predicate. Both cola keep the same two-word subject-plus-modifier shape.

rationale: The wicked's desire for evildoers' plunder opens the line; the waw swings to the root of the righteous, which is said to yield or give. rationale: Transgression of the lips sets a trap in the A-colon; a vav-consecutive wayyiqtol, וַיֵּצֵ֖א (oshb:Prov.12.13, byte tier), redirects to the righteous, who comes out of trouble. rejected_alternative: Linking forward to the fruit-of-the-mouth verse was rejected: 12:14 uses a different noun for the mouth's output (fruit, not transgression), and though it does carry a waw (וּגְמ֥וּל, oshb:Prov.12.14, byte tier), that conjunction's force is continuative rather than adversative, since 12:14 forms a synonymous, not antithetic, couplet.

rationale: One who breathes out faithfulness declares what is right in the A-colon; the waw turns to a lying witness, whose output is deceit. Courtroom vocabulary (witness, testify) opens here and continues into the next two verses without this verse itself sharing an exact token with either.

rationale: Both verses close on the exact same noun for tongue -- וּלְשׁ֖וֹן (oshb:Prov.12.18) and לְשׁ֣וֹן (oshb:Prov.12.19), byte tier -- both governing an opposite predicate: reckless speech is likened to a sword's stabbing before the wise tongue is called healing (12:18), and truthful lips are established while a tongue of falsehood lasts merely a moment (12:19). Both verses are already complete antithetic sentences on their own -- the grouping rests on nothing beyond the repeated noun linking two adjacent, independently closed couplets, so the cohesion evidence is thin.
rejected_alternative: Keeping these as two separate stand-alone rows was the default and was reconsidered because of the repeated tongue-noun; the shared term is one content token rather than a construction run, so the cluster call is registered at reduced confidence rather than dropped outright.

device_notes: Antithetic parallelism in both cola of both verses; catchword-cluster with a one-token chain (tongue), matching the thinner-than-two-token evidence class also disclosed at Prov.13.19-Prov.13.20. The tongue-noun (לשון) sits as the second-to-last word of its own colon in both verses, not verse-final. The falsehood-root recurs between this row's own 12:19 (שָֽׁקֶר, oshb:Prov.12.19, byte tier) and the immediately preceding 12:17 (שְׁקָרִ֣ים, oshb:Prov.12.17, byte tier); the atomic cluster boundary still holds despite this cross-seam tie, since 12:17 is itself a complete antithetic sentence with its own subject, distinct from 12:18-12:19's tongue-pair. The sword root occurs in 5 verses book-wide (Prov.5.4, Prov.12.18, Prov.17.1, Prov.25.18, Prov.30.14); of these, 4 are sword-class (5.4, 12.18, 25.18, 30.14) and 1 (17.1) is the dry-morsel homograph -- this verse's simile is one of the 4 book-wide sword-class occurrences, not one of a chapter-wide five.

rationale: Deceit sits in the heart of evil's devisers in the A-colon; the waw pivots to counselors of peace, whose reward is joy. The waw still marks the turn to the wicked, whose own way leads them astray, so the antithetic frame itself is not in doubt even where the opening verb's sense is.

That pointing distinction is the verse's own tier-1 evidence and closes the sentence as a synonymous reinforcement of life rather than a contrast with it.

rationale: The unit opens the words-of-the-wise collection with a double attention-imperative, הַ֥ט אָזְנְךָ֗ (oshb:Prov.22.17, 'turn your ear'), paired with וּ֭שְׁמַע (oshb:Prov.22.17, 'and listen'), and the phrase דִּבְרֵ֣י חֲכָמִ֑ים (oshb:Prov.22.17, 'words of the wise') sits mid-verse rather than as a separate header line, so the seam is argued from the clause itself and not from a title. Verse 19 states the address's purpose in an infinitive clause, לִהְי֣וֹת בַּ֭יהוָה (oshb:Prov.22.19, 'so that your trust may be in Yahweh'), and verses 20-21 restate that purpose with two further purpose infinitives, לְהוֹדִֽיעֲךָ֗ and לְהָשִׁ֥יב (oshb:Prov.22.21). The unit closes with a petuchah/pe seg (oshb:Prov.22.21, single-witness), corroborating the move into the content admonitions that open at 22:22. Verse 20 itself carries an unresolved ketiv/qere crux: the consonantal ketiv שלשום against the pointed qere שָׁלִישִׁ֑ים (oshb:Prov.22.20, ketiv/qere, single-witness) leaves the numeral/rank term underlying 'thirty' versus an officer-class reading undecided by the bytes; this row reports the crux without resolving it. Prov.23.1 (web:Prov.23.1-Prov.23.1) opens an unrelated court-and-dining scenario sharing no skeleton token with 22:17-22:21, corroborating this unit's close at the 22:21 petuchah rather than continuing it.
rejected_alternative: Reading 22:17 as a bare title line parallel to the mishle headers was set aside because the divrei-hakhamim wording sits inside the sentence's own grammar, not in a superscription position.

device_notes: Address-function-unified across the five verses, but grammatically two governing movements: an imperative address in vv.17-18 (הַ֥ט אָזְנְךָ֗/וּ֭שְׁמַע, oshb:Prov.22.17) with its own motive at v.18 (כִּֽי נָ֭עִים, oshb:Prov.22.18, 'for it is pleasant'), then a first-person disclosure in vv.19-21 built on הוֹדַעְתִּ֖יךָ (oshb:Prov.22.19) and כָתַ֣בְתִּי (oshb:Prov.22.20, ketiv/qere, single-witness), whose two infinitives at v.21 (לְהוֹדִֽיעֲךָ֗, לְהָשִׁ֥יב, oshb:Prov.22.21) attach as purpose clauses to v.20's verb -- a texture distinct from the sentence-literature run that follows in 23:1 onward.

rationale: A fresh imperative pair opens the verse, אַֽל תִּגְזָל (oshb:Prov.22.22, 'do not rob/exploit the poor'), directly after the petuchah/pe close of the prologue (oshb:Prov.22.21, single-witness); the topic itself changes from the collection's own purpose to a concrete social prohibition, marking the start of a new unit rather than a continuation. Verse 23 supplies the grounding motive with כִּֽי (oshb:Prov.22.23, 'for Yahweh will plead their case'), the standard imperative-plus-motive shape.
rejected_alternative: Folding this pair into the prologue was rejected since the prologue's own purpose clauses end at 22:21 and this couplet opens a distinct social-ethics topic.

rationale: אַל תִּ֭תְרַע (oshb:Prov.22.24, 'do not befriend a hot-tempered man') opens a new prohibition unrelated to the court-justice topic just closed; verse 25 supplies a purpose clause, פֶּן תֶּאֱלַ֥ף (oshb:Prov.22.25, 'lest you learn his ways'), completing a two-verse imperative-plus-purpose unit. rationale: אַל תַּ֭סֵּג גְּב֣וּל עוֹלָ֑ם (oshb:Prov.22.28, 'do not move the ancient boundary stone') is a bare second-person vetitive governing the whole verse, closed by a relative clause naming the fathers who set the boundary, אֲשֶׁ֖ר עָשׂ֣וּ אֲבוֹתֶֽיךָ (oshb:Prov.22.28) -- the relative clause names an authority for the boundary rather than supplying a motive clause, distinguishing this admonition_unit from the imperative-plus-motive shape used elsewhere in the span. The same vetitive recurs byte-identical in its first four words, אַל תַּ֭סֵּג גְּב֣וּל עוֹלָ֑ם (oshb:Prov.23.10), where a second prohibition and an added motive clause build the fuller two-verse admonition at 23:10-11; this row's one-verse span is argued on its own bytes, not as an abbreviation of that later restatement.

Reading it as an admonition_unit opener continuing into 22:29 was also rejected, since 22:29 shifts to an unrelated observation about skilled workers, sharing no vocabulary with the boundary-stone maxim.

a conditional is answered by the father's joy, restated at verse 16 (Prov.23.15, Prov.23.16)
device_notes: A first-person father-speech unit rather than a second-person prohibition; synthetic parallelism (condition, then joy, then intensified restatement).

rationale: אַל יְקַנֵּ֣א לִ֭בְּךָ (oshb:Prov.23.17, 'do not let your heart envy sinners') opens a fresh prohibition after the father's-joy unit closes at 23:16; the same verse supplies its own contrastive motive, כִּ֥י אִם (oshb:Prov.23.17, 'but rather fear Yahweh'), and verse 18 closes with a hope clause, וְ֝תִקְוָתְךָ֗ לֹ֣א תִכָּרֵֽת (oshb:Prov.23.18, 'your hope will not be cut off'); the same wording recurs at Prov.24.13-Prov.24.14, a non-adjacent refrain rather than a device local to this pair.
rejected_alternative: Treating verse 18 as a detached single_proverb about future hope was rejected because its subject depends on the envy prohibition verse 17 states rather than standing on its own.
observed_substrate_signals: a prohibition-plus-contrast falls within verse 17 (Prov.23.17)
a hope clause closes verse 18, the same wording recurring at 24:14 (Prov.23.18)
device_notes: The hope-not-cut-off clause is a book-internal refrain (23:18 and 24:13-14 share the exact wording); noted here as texture, not as a boundary argument for either row.

rationale: A second vocative address opens the unit, שְׁמַע אַתָּ֣ה בְנִ֣י (oshb:Prov.23.19, 'listen, you, my son'), distinct from the 23:15 vocative by its own topic (right paths, then drunkenness); verse 20 issues the prohibition אַל תְּהִ֥י בְסֹֽבְאֵי יָ֑יִן (oshb:Prov.23.20, 'do not be among winebibbers'), and verse 21 supplies the motive with כִּי (oshb:Prov.23.21, 'for the drunkard and glutton will grow poor'), closing a three-verse vocative-plus-motive unit.
rejected_alternative: Reading 23:19 as a continuation of the 23:15-16 address was rejected because a fresh vocative reopens the address and the topic moves from filial joy to wine and meat.
observed_substrate_signals: a vocative reopens the address (Prov.23.19)
a prohibition against drunkenness follows (Prov.23.20)
a motive clause closes the unit (Prov.23.21)
device_notes: Vocative-opened admonition_unit; the drunkard/glutton pairing anticipates the fuller wine poem beginning at 23:29.

rationale: שְׁמַ֣ע לְ֭אָבִיךָ (oshb:Prov.23.22, 'listen to your father') opens a paired positive-and-negative command about parents, closed within the same verse by a motive clause, כִּֽי זָקְנָ֥ה (oshb:Prov.23.22, 'for she is old'). The topic (parents) does not continue the drunkenness warning just closed, and 23:23's command to buy truth opens a distinct topic after it, so the verse stands as its own compressed unit.
rejected_alternative: Grouping this verse with 23:24-25's father's-joy couplet was set aside: the father/mother root does recur across the span (23:22, 23:24, 23:25 -- 3 verses), but 23:23's buy-the-truth maxim between them opens its own distinct commerce topic sharing that root with neither neighbor, an independently sufficient ground for keeping 23:22 a standalone unit.
observed_substrate_signals: a paired command about parents with an internal motive clause (Prov.23.22)
device_notes: Command-plus-motive compressed to one verse, matching the shape used for 23:9.

rationale: אֱמֶ֣ת קְ֭נֵה וְאַל תִּמְכֹּ֑ר (oshb:Prov.23.23, 'buy the truth, and do not sell it') is a governing second-person imperative-plus-vetitive command filling the whole verse -- קְ֭נֵה an imperative, וְאַל תִּמְכֹּ֑ר a vetitive -- lacking a following motive clause. No exact wordform repeats at either seam; the honor-your-parents command before it (oshb:Prov.23.22) shares no root, while the father's-joy couplet after it does share a cognate: the wisdom root named here in חָכְמָ֖ה (oshb:Prov.23.23) recurs in nominal form as חָ֝כָ֗ם (oshb:Prov.23.24; word-bound exact token, 26/915 verses book-wide) -- a textural echo, not a shared boundary word.
rejected_alternative: Reading the verse as a single_proverb on the strength of its lacking a motive clause was set aside: the mood test C3 applies to its admonition_unit default fires on the governing imperative-plus-vetitive frame regardless of a following motive clause, and admonition_unit is the value that fits wherever that frame governs the span.
observed_substrate_signals: a governing imperative-plus-vetitive command fills the whole verse (Prov.23.23)
no exact wordform repeats at either seam; a cognate wisdom root recurs at 23:24 (word-bound exact token, 26/915 book-wide)
device_notes: A self-contained commercial-metaphor command (buy/do not sell) rather than a bare maxim; the imperative-plus-vetitive frame governs the whole span even without a motive clause.

rationale: Verse 24 carries four ketiv/qere pairs in one line -- גול/גִּ֣יל, יגול/יָ֭גִיל, יולד/וְיוֹלֵ֥ד, וישמח/יִשְׂמַח (oshb:Prov.23.24, ketiv/qere, single-witness) -- and its qere verb יִשְׂמַח recurs at the head of verse 25, יִֽשְׂמַח אָבִ֥יךָ וְאִמֶּ֑ךָ (oshb:Prov.23.25, 'let your father and mother be glad'), the shared root binding the general maxim about a righteous child's parent to its applied wish for this son's own parents.
rejected_alternative: Reading verse 24 alone as the row and verse 25 as a separate single_proverb was considered, given the topical shift from general maxim to direct wish, but was set aside because the repeated root binds the two into one developing statement.
observed_substrate_signals: four ketiv/qere pairs sit in one verse (Prov.23.24, single-witness)
the qere verb at 23:24 recurs as the opening verb of 23:25
device_notes: Synthetic pair: general maxim, then its personalized application, joined by a repeated root; the K/Q density leaves the exact wording of verse 24 less certain than the boundary decision itself. Both יָ֭גִיל (oshb:Prov.23.24, ketiv/qere, single-witness) and יִֽשְׂמַח (oshb:Prov.23.25) are third-person jussive wishes about the parents' own joy, not a governing second-person imperative or vetitive, so the span stands outside C3's operative admonition_unit category by its own grammar.

rationale: A third vocative opens the unit, תְּנָֽה בְנִ֣י לִבְּךָ֣ לִ֑י (oshb:Prov.23.26, 'give me your heart, my son'), carrying its own ketiv/qere note, תרצנה/תִּצֹּֽרְנָה (oshb:Prov.23.26, ketiv/qere, single-witness); verse 27 supplies the motive with כִּֽי (oshb:Prov.23.27) and the deep-pit/narrow-well image for the unfaithful wife, and verse 28 continues that image, closing a three-verse vocative-plus-motive unit that reads as the collection's compressed version of the strange-woman warnings developed at length in chapters 1-9.
rejected_alternative: Stopping the unit at verse 26 alone was rejected because the motive clause of verse 27 supplies the rationale the vocative command needs, and verse 28 continues rather than restarts that image.
observed_substrate_signals: a vocative and imperative open the unit, with a ketiv/qere note (Prov.23.26, single-witness)
a motive clause with the deep-pit image follows (Prov.23.27)
device_notes: A vocative-plus-motive admonition on the strange woman, structurally the same shape as 23:19-21 but on a different topic.

rationale: Seven verses build one extended treatment rather than a chain of couplets: verse 29 opens with a six-fold rhetorical לְמִ֨י (oshb:Prov.23.29, 'who has...?') list naming woe, sorrow, and wounds, itself carrying a ketiv/qere pair at its fourth item, מדונים מִדְיָנִ֨ים (oshb:Prov.23.29, ketiv/qere, single-witness); verse 30 answers the riddle (those who linger over wine); verse 31 supplies the span's one negative command, אַל תֵּ֥רֶא יַיִן֮ (oshb:Prov.23.31, 'do not look at the wine'), itself carrying a ketiv/qere pair, בכיס/בַּכּ֣וֹס (oshb:Prov.23.31, ketiv/qere, single-witness); and verses 32-35 describe the aftermath in extended imagery, closing with the drunkard's own quoted words at verse 35. The riddle-form opening and the closing quoted speech mark this as a poem rather than an imperative admonition stretched past its usual two-to-four-verse span.
rejected_alternative: Segmenting the span into shorter admonition_unit rows (29-30, 31, 32-35) was considered but rejected because the six-fold riddle of verse 29 is answered across the full span, not resolved within any short sub-unit.
observed_substrate_signals: a six-fold rhetorical list opens the span, itself K/Q-marked at its fourth item (Prov.23.29, single-witness)
the span's one negative command sits at verse 31, itself K/Q-marked (Prov.23.31, single-witness)
the drunkard's own quoted speech closes the span at verse 35
device_notes: Riddle-question opening, descriptive middle, first-person quoted close -- the formal shape recognized elsewhere in the book's set-piece poems, here on drunkenness; chapter boundaries fall cleanly on both sides. The span's one second-person vetitive at v.31 sits embedded inside the poem's own riddle-and-answer shape rather than governing the span's structure, so the span stands outside C3's operative admonition_unit category by its own grammar despite carrying a vetitive.

rationale: The chapter opens with אַל תְּ֭קַנֵּא בְּאַנְשֵׁ֣י רָעָ֑ה (oshb:Prov.24.1, 'do not envy evil men'), a fresh topic after the wine poem closes at 23:35, carrying its own ketiv/qere note, תתאו/תִּ֝תְאָ֗יו (oshb:Prov.24.1, ketiv/qere, single-witness); verse 2 supplies the motive with כִּי (oshb:Prov.24.2, 'for their hearts plot violence'). The same verb root recurs at Prov.24.19, a non-adjacent bracketing of the chapter's opening and closing prohibitions rather than a link within this pair.
rejected_alternative: Extending the unit to include verse 3's wisdom-builds-a-house maxim was rejected because verse 3 shares no root with the envy prohibition and opens a distinct declarative topic.
observed_substrate_signals: a prohibition opens the chapter, with a ketiv/qere note (Prov.24.1, single-witness)
a motive clause follows at verse 2 (Prov.24.2)
the same verb root recurs at 24:19, bracketing the chapter's open with a later prohibition rather than binding to this pair
device_notes: Standard prohibition-plus-motive shape; the recurrence of the envy-verb at 24:19 is noted as texture, not as grounds to widen this row.

rationale: בְּ֭חָכְמָה יִבָּ֣נֶה בָּ֑יִת (oshb:Prov.24.3, 'through wisdom a house is built') opens a declarative image rather than an imperative; verse 4 continues the same house image with חֲדָרִ֣ים (oshb:Prov.24.4, 'rooms... filled'), the shared building-image vocabulary (house, established, rooms) binding the pair as one developing figure rather than two unrelated maxims.
rejected_alternative: Reading verses 3 and 4 as two separate single_proverb rows was set aside because verse 4's rooms-filled-with-treasure image completes rather than restarts the house-building figure verse 3 opens.
observed_substrate_signals: a house-building image opens the pair (Prov.24.3)
the same image continues at verse 4 (rooms filled with treasure)
device_notes: Declarative synthetic pair; יִבָּ֣נֶה and יִתְכּוֹנָֽן (oshb:Prov.24.3) are third-person Niphal passives, not a governing second-person imperative or vetitive, so it stands outside C3's operative admonition_unit category by its own grammar; wisdom's practical benefit shown through the house figure.

rationale: גֶּֽבֶר חָכָ֥ם בַּע֑וֹז (oshb:Prov.24.5, 'a wise man is in strength') opens a strength/power image distinct from the house-building figure just closed at 24:4; verse 6 opens with the causal particle כִּ֣י (oshb:Prov.24.6, 'for'), its clause בְ֭תַחְבֻּלוֹת תַּעֲשֶׂה לְּךָ֣ מִלְחָמָ֑ה ('by strategies you wage war') explaining how the wise man's strength in v.5 is exercised -- a motive-clause warrant, not a repeated-vocabulary one.
rejected_alternative: Reading 24:5-6 as a continuation of the 24:3-4 house-building cluster was rejected since no building-vocabulary token repeats past verse 4, and the strength/war image opens its own figure at verse 5.
observed_substrate_signals: a strength image opens the pair (Prov.24.5)
a war/counsel motive explains it (Prov.24.6)
device_notes: A second wisdom's-benefit cluster (strength/war) immediately following the house-building cluster; no building-vocabulary token repeats past v4, and the common wisdom-root (דַּ֝֗עַת) that recurs across the 24:4|24:5 seam (וּ֭בְדַעַת, oshb:Prov.24.4; וְאִֽישׁ דַּ֝֗עַת, oshb:Prov.24.5) is textural (44/915 verses book-wide, one of five adjacent-verse pairs the root forms across the book), not an independent catchword. v.5 is a nominal predication and v.6's תַּעֲשֶׂה (oshb:Prov.24.6) a gnomic/generic imperfect, not a governing second-person imperative or vetitive, so the span stands outside C3's operative admonition_unit category by its own grammar.

rationale: רָאמ֣וֹת לֶֽאֱוִ֣יל חָכְמ֑וֹת (oshb:Prov.24.7, 'wisdom is too high for a fool') states a complete observation about the fool's exclusion from the gate-council; it shares no root with the strength/war image before it or the scheme/mockery pair after it, so it stands as its own maxim between two clusters.
rejected_alternative: Reading this verse as opening the following scheme/mockery cluster was set aside because the fool and the mocker are named with distinct social-type terms sharing no root across the seam.
observed_substrate_signals: a declarative maxim shares no root with either neighbor (Prov.24.7)
device_notes: Declarative one-verse maxim on the fool's exclusion from public deliberation. רָאמ֣וֹת (oshb:Prov.24.7) is a nominal predication, not a second-person imperative or vetitive, so it stands outside C3's operative admonition_unit category by its own grammar.

rationale: מְחַשֵּׁ֥ב לְהָרֵ֑עַ (oshb:Prov.24.8, 'one who plots evil') is called מְזִמּ֥וֹת (oshb:Prov.24.8, 'a man of schemes'); verse 9 opens with the same consonantal root, זִמַּ֣ת אִוֶּ֣לֶת (oshb:Prov.24.9, 'the scheme of folly is sin'), the repeated root binding the schemer-maxim to the mocker-maxim that follows it in the same verse.
rejected_alternative: Splitting verse 9 into its own single_proverb was rejected because its opening word repeats verse 8's scheme-root rather than opening an unrelated topic.
observed_substrate_signals: a scheme-root recurs across the seam, at verse 8 and again at verse 9 (Prov.24.8, Prov.24.9)
device_notes: Catchword-bound cluster on the scheming mind, moving from the plotter himself to his plotting's classification as sin. A participle names the plotter in v.8 and a nominal sentence classifies the scheme in v.9 -- neither a second-person imperative nor a vetitive -- so the span stands outside C3's operative admonition_unit category by its own grammar.

rationale: הִ֭תְרַפִּיתָ בְּי֥וֹם צָרָ֗ה (oshb:Prov.24.10, 'if you falter in a day of distress, your strength is small') states a complete conditional maxim about personal resilience, sharing no root with the scheming/mockery pair before it or the rescue command after it.
rejected_alternative: Grouping this verse with the rescue command at 24:11-12 was set aside because it addresses the reader's own faltering rather than the reader's duty toward a third party being led to death.
observed_substrate_signals: a conditional maxim on personal resilience shares no root with either neighbor (Prov.24.10)
device_notes: A self-contained conditional maxim, its own topic (personal strength under distress) bridging two unrelated units. Its verb הִ֭תְרַפִּיתָ (oshb:Prov.24.10) is a perfect-tense conditional protasis, not an imperative or vetitive, so it stands outside C3's operative admonition_unit category by its own grammar.

rationale: הַ֭צֵּל לְקֻחִ֣ים לַמָּ֑וֶת (oshb:Prov.24.11, 'rescue those being led away to death') is an imperative command; verse 12 anticipates and answers an excuse, תֹאמַ֗ר...הֲֽלֹא (oshb:Prov.24.12), functioning as the unit's motive by showing that the excuse fails, since God weighs hearts and repays deeds.
rejected_alternative: Reading verse 12 as an independent single_proverb about divine judgment was rejected because its opening clause answers the specific excuse the rescue-command of verse 11 anticipates.
observed_substrate_signals: an imperative command opens the unit (Prov.24.11)
verse 12 rebuts an anticipated excuse rather than opening a new topic (Prov.24.12)
device_notes: Imperative-plus-rebutted-excuse shape, one of the few spots in this span where the motive verse takes the form of an answered objection rather than a plain motive clause.

rationale: A vocative reopens the address, אֱכָל בְּנִ֣י דְבַ֣שׁ (oshb:Prov.24.13, 'eat honey, my son'), after two verses without one; verse 14 applies the honey image to wisdom with כֵּ֤ן דְּעֶ֥ה (oshb:Prov.24.14, 'so know wisdom for your soul') and closes with the hope-not-cut-off clause, וְ֝תִקְוָתְךָ֗ לֹ֣א תִכָּרֵֽת (oshb:Prov.24.14), that recurs, with the same wording, at Prov.23.17-Prov.23.18. A petuchah/pe seg follows verse 14 (oshb:Prov.24.14, single-witness), corroborating the move into the wicked-man warning at 24:15.
rejected_alternative: Reading verse 13 alone as a single_proverb about honey was rejected because its taste-image sets up verse 14's applied purpose clause rather than standing complete on its own.
observed_substrate_signals: a vocative reopens the address (Prov.24.13)
a purpose clause applies the honey image to wisdom (Prov.24.14)
the hope-not-cut-off clause repeats the exact wording of 23:18
petuchah/pe seg closes the unit (Prov.24.14, single-witness)
device_notes: Vocative-plus-applied-purpose shape; the hope refrain shared with 23:18 is texture linking two rows without collapsing either boundary.

rationale: The unit opens right after the petuchah/pe seg at 24:14 (oshb:Prov.24.14, single-witness) with a direct address to a named wrongdoer, אַל תֶּאֱרֹ֣ב רָ֭שָׁע (oshb:Prov.24.15, 'do not lie in wait, wicked one'); verse 16 supplies the motive with כִּ֤י (oshb:Prov.24.16) and the righteous-falls-and-rises antithesis, closing the two-verse unit.
rejected_alternative: Reading verse 16 as a detached single_proverb on the righteous falling seven times was rejected because its motive clause exists to ground the prohibition verse 15 addresses to the wicked man.
observed_substrate_signals: a direct address to the wrongdoer opens the prohibition (Prov.24.15)
a motive clause with the falls-and-rises antithesis follows (Prov.24.16)
petuchah/pe at the immediately preceding verse (Prov.24.14, single-witness)
device_notes: Antithetic motive clause (righteous rises / wicked overthrown) grounding a direct-address prohibition.

rationale: בִּנְפֹ֣ל (oshb:Prov.24.17, 'when...falls') opens a fresh prohibition addressed to the reader in the second person, a register shift from the third-person wicked-man narration just closed at 24:16 (כִּ֤י שֶׁ֨בַע יִפּ֣וֹל צַדִּ֣יק וָקָ֑ם וּ֝רְשָׁעִ֗ים יִכָּשְׁל֥וּ בְרָעָֽה, oshb:Prov.24.16, 'a righteous man falls seven times and rises, but the wicked stumble in calamity'). The seam carries two root-echoes disclosed as texture rather than a boundary driver: כשל recurs adjacently at both verses (יִכָּשְׁל֥וּ, oshb:Prov.24.16; וּ֝בִכָּשְׁל֗וֹ, oshb:Prov.24.17 -- 6/915 book-wide, the sole adjacent pair among those hits), and נפל recurs in a different surface form each time (יִפּ֣וֹל, oshb:Prov.24.16, the assimilated Niphal-pattern imperfect losing its נ; בִּנְפֹ֣ל, oshb:Prov.24.17, the unassimilated infinitive construct retaining it -- 2/915 book-wide at the byte-skeleton tier). This row's object carries a ketiv/qere note, אויביך/אֽ֭וֹיִבְךָ (oshb:Prov.24.17, ketiv/qere, single-witness), before the prohibition itself, אַל תִּשְׂמָ֑ח (oshb:Prov.24.17, 'do not rejoice'); verse 18 supplies the motive with פֶּן (oshb:Prov.24.18, 'lest Yahweh see it and turn his wrath').
rejected_alternative: Merging this pair with the 24:19-20 envy prohibition into one four-verse unit was set aside because a fresh imperative reopens at 24:19 with its own motive rather than continuing this one. Extending the unit backward to absorb 24:15-16 was also considered, given the shared כשל/נפל root-echoes at the seam (oshb:Prov.24.16, oshb:Prov.24.17), but was set aside because 24:17 shifts from third-person wicked-man narration to a direct second-person address the earlier verses do not carry, a positive register change rather than mere restatement.
observed_substrate_signals: a prohibition opens the pair, with a ketiv/qere note at its object (Prov.24.17, single-witness)
a motive clause follows at verse 18 (Prov.24.18)
device_notes: Prohibition-plus-motive shape, the enemy's fall framed as a test of the reader's own character rather than a legal or commercial scene.

rationale: אַל תִּתְחַ֥ר (oshb:Prov.24.19, 'do not fret') opens a doubled prohibition, continued after its object by אַל תְּ֝קַנֵּ֗א (oshb:Prov.24.19, 'do not envy the wicked'); verse 20 supplies the motive with כִּ֤י (oshb:Prov.24.20, 'the evil man's future holds no reward, the wicked man's lamp is snuffed out'). The second verb repeats the chapter's opening prohibition at Prov.24.1, the same root bracketing the chapter's opening unit and this later one without merging them.
rejected_alternative: Reading this pair as a continuation of the 24:17-18 enemy's-fall prohibition was rejected because a fresh doubled imperative reopens at 24:19 rather than extending verse 18's purpose clause.
observed_substrate_signals: a doubled prohibition opens the pair (Prov.24.19)
a motive clause with the snuffed-lamp image follows (Prov.24.20)
the envy-verb recurs from 24:1, bracketing rather than joining the two units
device_notes: The envy-verb frames the chapter's own units (24:1-2 and 24:19-20) at a distance; recorded as texture, not as grounds to widen either row.

rationale: The chapter's closing vocative opens the unit, יְרָֽא אֶת יְהוָ֣ה בְּנִ֣י (oshb:Prov.24.21, 'fear Yahweh, my son') continued by וָמֶ֑לֶךְ (oshb:Prov.24.21, 'and the king'); verse 22 supplies the motive with כִּֽי (oshb:Prov.24.22, 'for their calamity will rise suddenly'). The verse closes the C3 collection, and a setumah/samekh seg sits at this verse (oshb:Prov.24.22, single-witness), the book's one setumah seg total, corroborating at tier-3 the seam this row's own vocative-plus-motive grammar already argues at tier-1.
rejected_alternative: Reading verse 22 as opening the C4 appendix rather than closing this unit was rejected because its motive clause grounds the fear-Yahweh-and-king command of verse 21 rather than introducing the heading that follows.
observed_substrate_signals: a vocative and imperative open the closing unit of C3 (Prov.24.21)
a motive clause closes it (Prov.24.22)
a setumah/samekh seg sits at the closing verse, 1 of 52 parashah segs total (Prov.24.22, single-witness)
device_notes: The collection's final vocative-plus-motive admonition; the setumah seg corroborates without driving the boundary already argued from the grammar.

rationale: גַּם אֵ֥לֶּה (oshb:Prov.24.23, 'also these') opens the C4 appendix immediately after the setumah/samekh seg at 24:22 (oshb:Prov.24.22, single-witness); the heading's own maxim, הַֽכֵּר פָּנִ֖ים בְּמִשְׁפָּ֣ט (oshb:Prov.24.23, 'to show partiality in judgment is not good'), is illustrated by verse 24's case of calling the wicked righteous and resolved by verse 25's adversative, וְלַמּוֹכִיחִ֥ים (oshb:Prov.24.25, 'but to those who convict, it will be pleasant'), the three verses forming one developing statement on judicial partiality rather than a bare header plus two unrelated maxims.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the header at 24:23 into its own row from the illustration at 24:24-25 was considered, on the model of the mishle headers elsewhere, but was set aside because 24:23 already states a complete partiality maxim that 24:24-25 illustrates and resolves rather than merely labels.
observed_substrate_signals: the heading opens with its own complete maxim (Prov.24.23)
an adversative resolves the case at verse 25 (Prov.24.25)
a setumah/samekh seg sits at the immediately preceding verse (Prov.24.22, single-witness)
device_notes: Antithetic close (curse on the partial judge, blessing on the one who convicts) built out from a heading-maxim rather than a plain antithetic couplet. Confidence is held at medium_low because the three-verse reading rests on treating 24:23's heading-maxim as joined to its own illustration and resolution rather than as a free-standing header verse, the pattern the book's other headers follow elsewhere.

rationale: שְׂפָתַ֥יִם יִשָּׁ֑ק (oshb:Prov.24.26, 'he kisses the lips') paired with מֵ֝שִׁ֗יב דְּבָרִ֥ים נְכֹחִֽים (oshb:Prov.24.26, 'who gives a right answer') is a self-contained simile about honest speech, sharing no root with the judicial-partiality unit before it or the field-work command after it.
rejected_alternative: Reading this verse as closing the judicial-partiality cluster at 24:23-25 was rejected because its subject moves from courtroom testimony to speech ethics generally, sharing no vocabulary that bridges the seam.

rationale: אַל תֹּאמַ֗ר (oshb:Prov.24.29, 'do not say') opens a forbidden planned speech-act of revenge, completed by כַּאֲשֶׁ֣ר עָֽשָׂה לִ֭י כֵּ֤ן אֶֽעֱשֶׂה לּ֑וֹ (oshb:Prov.24.29, 'as he did to me so I will do to him'), complete in one verse, lacking a motive clause and sharing no root with the false-witness maxim before it. It does share the איש root with the sluggard's-field vignette after it -- אָשִׁ֖יב לָאִ֣ישׁ (oshb:Prov.24.29) and שְׂדֵ֣ה אִישׁ (oshb:Prov.24.30; 87/915 verses book-wide) -- disclosed here as non-driving cross-seam texture; the boundary instead rests on the register shift from 24:29's quoted forbidden speech to 24:30's first-person narrative opening.

Grouping it backward with 24:28's false-witness prohibition was also considered, since both share an אל-plus-prohibited-speech construction (אַל תְּהִ֣י עֵד, oshb:Prov.24.28; אַל תֹּאמַ֗ר, oshb:Prov.24.29), but was set aside because the two name distinct wrongs -- false testimony against a third party versus private retaliatory speech -- rather than one developing prohibition.

rationale: The verse opens the second Solomonic collection with the skeleton-initial phrase גַּם אֵ֭לֶּה (oshb:Prov.25.1) ("also these"), the second of exactly two verse-initial gam-elleh sites in the book (the other, outside this part, is 24:23), and carries the interior word מִשְׁלֵ֣י (oshb:Prov.25.1) ("proverbs of"), one of exactly three mishle-anywhere sites (1:1, 10:1 verse-initial; 25:1 interior). rationale: The two verses share the exact skeleton token מְ֝לָכִ֗ים (oshb:Prov.25.2) / מְ֝לָכִ֗ים (oshb:Prov.25.3) ("kings", plural) and the root חקר ("search"), realized as the infinitive חֲקֹ֣ר (oshb:Prov.25.2) in v2 and the noun חֵֽקֶר (oshb:Prov.25.3) in v3. v2 states the principle that kings' matters are for searching out; v3 supplies the illustration (heaven's height, earth's depth) that makes the kings' heart categorically unsearchable. A targeted sweep of this part's skeletons finds the plural form at 2 of the part's 83 verses (25:2 and 25:3), distinct from the singular used of the historical king in 25:1, 25:5, 25:6.

rationale: The unit opens on the book's second and final divrei-plus-massa header, דִּ֭בְרֵי לְמוּאֵ֣ל מֶ֑לֶךְ מַ֝שָּׂ֗א (oshb:Prov.31.1, "the words of Lemuel the king, an oracle"), matching web:Prov.30.1 in kind (the same opening token דִּ֭בְרֵי pairs with an oracle-word as an actual header in 2 of the 19 book-wide hits, sweep: 2 of 19) though never in wording. The mother's address that follows opens with a triple vocative on a short root, מַה בְּ֭רִי וּמַֽה בַּר בִּטְנִ֑י וּ֝מֶה בַּר נְדָרָֽי (oshb:Prov.31.2, "what, my son! what, son of my womb! what, son of my vows!") -- the later two vocatives here, בַּר and בַּר, use a short form beside the fuller בְּ֭רִי used earlier in the same verse; that short form is Aramaic-influenced address vocabulary, discussion material rather than a claim that the verse itself is in Aramaic (every morph code in the book is H-prefixed, sweep: 6984 of 6984). The same address continues through the warnings against wine and women (31:3-7, including the twice-repeated אַ֤ל לַֽמְלָכִ֨ים לְֽמוֹאֵ֗ל אַ֣ל לַֽמְלָכִ֣ים at oshb:Prov.31.4, ketiv/qere verse, "not for kings ... not for kings") into the closing charge to judge the poor justly (31:8-9); the petuchah at oshb:Prov.31.9 (single-witness, disclosed) is the unit's one interior mark, closing it right before the acrostic begins.
rejected_alternative: Splitting the wine warning (31:3-7) from the justice charge (31:8-9) into two admonition_unit rows was considered, since their imagery differs, but across 31:2-8, four of the seven verses carry the mother's direct singular address (31:2 vocative address; 31:3 2ms prohibition; 31:4 vocative לְֽמוֹאֵ֗ל (oshb:Prov.31.4, ketiv/qere verse) plus infinitive; 31:8 2ms imperative), while three depart from it within the same wine-warning topic (31:5, 31:7: 3ms narrative describing an unnamed king-figure; 31:6: 2mp imperative to a different addressee) -- the one-unit reading holds on the petuchah bracket (oshb:Prov.30.33 and oshb:Prov.31.9, both single-witness) and the address-envelope spanning 31:2 to 31:8, not on uniform address verse by verse.
